strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing genuine limitations of prior work (single-joint assumptions, pre-specified part counts)
Elegant latent-conditioned deformation field that unifies geometry, appearance, and kinematics in a single representation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with extended PartNet-Mobility benchmark and new RS-Art real-to-sim dataset
Consistent quantitative improvements over four SOTA baselines across multiple metrics (axis angle/position, motion parameters, Chamfer distance)
Strong generalization capability: method can interpolate latent codes to generate smooth trajectories for unseen interaction states
Thorough ablations demonstrating impact of refinement stage (35-60% geometry improvement) and number of interaction states
Dataset contribution (RS-Art) valuable for bridging sim-to-real gap with high-quality ground truth (URDF format, physics properties)
Addresses practical problem relevant to robotics and digital twin applications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (latent-coded deformation of 3DGS, K-means clustering, SAM integration) without novel methodological advances
Problematic dependency on Visual Language Model for part count estimation contradicts 'fully self-supervised' claim; no analysis of VLM failure rates or robustness
Multiple ad-hoc hyperparameter choices (τ_mot, τ_vis=1.2, prompt split 10/20, joint type threshold r<0.05) lacking proper justification, ablations, or sensitivity analysis
Limited real-world evaluation: RS-Art contains only 18 objects (6 categories × 3 instances); only ArtGS compared on real data; other baselines 'failed to run' indicating robustness concerns
Coarse part segmentation quality not evaluated; heavy dependence on SAM mask quality and lack of graceful failure analysis when segmentation fails
Experimental comparison complicated by different input information distribution: single-part methods see clean per-joint motion; DeGSS sees coupled motion despite equal 'image budget'
Insufficient failure mode analysis: Section E (limitations) is brief; no concrete examples of when trajectory clustering fails, how to handle complex linkages or highly coupled joints
Real-world results show higher errors than synthetic (Table 4) with limited analysis of sim-to-real gap and domain transfer challenges
No computational cost analysis: missing training time, memory consumption, inference speed comparisons with baselines
Limited generalization scope: only simple rigid objects with revolute/prismatic joints tested; scalability to complex linkages, redundant articulation, or soft parts unclear
Requires accurate camera poses with no robustness analysis to pose noise; cannot reconstruct fully occluded regions
Statistical rigor lacking: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests; single run per method limits confidence in improvements
Limited ablations on critical design choices: motion descriptor formulation, MLP architecture for deformation network, K-means implementation details

strengths: Well-motivated unified framework using latent-conditioned continuous deformation of a canonical Gaussian field to handle multi-state articulated objects without manual part specification
Comprehensive experimental evaluation addressing key limitations of prior work: evaluates multiple instances per category (vs. single instance) and includes objects with 2-5 movable parts
Valuable dataset contribution (RS-Art): 18 objects with RGB-D captures, reverse-engineered URDF models, and joint annotations bridging synthetic and real scenarios
Strong empirical results across multiple metrics (geometry, kinematics) with consistent improvements over recent baselines (ArtGS, DTArt, PARIS, ArticulatedGS)
Extensive ablation studies validating each component (refinement stage, number of states, VLM prompting, SAM segmentation) and demonstrating robustness
Generalization to unseen interaction states via latent code interpolation outperforms dynamic NeRF/3DGS methods in rendering quality
Clear presentation with informative figures and logical pipeline design
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: deformable Gaussian Splatting via latent-conditioned MLPs, motion-based K-means clustering, and SAM-based refinement are each relatively standard; contribution is primarily in combination rather than new concepts or theoretical insights

Critical dependence on external tools (VLM for part counting, SAM for segmentation) introduces potential bottlenecks; lacks robustness analysis for VLM failures (e.g., predicting wrong part count); components not integrated into optimization

Strong camera pose assumptions with non-negligible degradation under pose errors (Table 8: axis angle 0.40→10.00 with 3.0° rotation noise); practical pose estimation strategies for articulated objects not discussed

Evaluation primarily synthetic: PartNet-Mobility has simple geometry; RS-Art controlled with limited real-world validation; quantitative metrics on real data sparse (Table 7) with 5-10× higher errors than synthetic; limited to simple articulation types

Ad-hoc design choices lack principled justification: 2% cluster threshold, visibility threshold τvis tuned on 1-2 instances, joint type rank ratio r<0.05; no theoretical grounding for why deformation trajectory clustering discovers semantically correct parts

Incomplete handling of occlusion: paper acknowledges inability to reconstruct fully occluded regions but provides no quantitative evaluation of segmentation accuracy under occlusion; for practical digital twins with self-occluding parts this is limiting

Scalability concerns: training time increases with parts; MLP inference cost per Gaussian not analyzed; no evaluation on >5 part objects or complex articulation; RS-Art dataset relatively small (18 objects, 6 categories)

Methodological issues: reporting only 'first run' for variance analysis (Table 1) complicates reproducibility; some metrics cluster near zero making comparison noisy; Chamfer distances vary wildly (0.02-143.78) suggesting unaccounted scale differences; comparison methodology not always fair (e.g., automatic vs. manual part specification)
